Show HN: Sync MacroFactor CSV to Obsidian for a Local Food Base Usable with AI
items.summary: I synchronized my MacroFactor CSV exports into a local-first, spreadsheet-free nutrition and food-asset database inside Obsidian (works on Desktop/iOS/Android and uses zero external APIs). The open-sourced template scripts help you make food decisions with recursive ingredient management and food queries which support 56-nutrients (macronutrients, vitamins, minerals, and amino acids). Here are technical details. - Food ID: Every food gets a Base36 hash ID (`food_<b36>`). - Same Name, Diff Macro resolution: The sync engine lets you resolve these conflicts in an Obsidian Base using frontmatter properties (`set_as_final_version`, `set_as_unique`, `duplicate_of`) without overriding user-defined notes or properties. - Recursive ingredient management: Foods contain an `[[Ingredient]]` property and any `banned` ingredient propagates on sync. Unbanning an ingredient also restores the ban state of an item before a propagated ban. The core MacroFactor food log and brand history synchronization template is MIT-licensed in the repository. The README also links to an optional pre-configured 40+ file Starter Vault with the Base UIs, a diet planner, double-entry ledger, and route generator (Dijkstra + TSP: for routes optimized by cost, time, kcal, etc). What other health, nutrition, or personal logs have you synced into a Markdown note system to use as structured context with AI and what problems are you solving with it?

items.title: Show HN: Turbotap – Open-Source CLI for AI Agents to Drive an iPhone over Wi-Fi
items.summary: I’ve been trying to make more of my daily life AI-driven, and my iPhone was becoming the bottleneck. If an app didn’t have a web version, an MCP, or an API, I still had to pick up the phone and do it myself. After lots of searching I finally found a solution that worked. I put a spare iPhone in developer mode, installed WebDriverAgent, and left it on my home Wi-Fi. WebDriverAgent is built on Apple’s official UI testing framework. It’s literally computer use for iPhone. I tried mirroring the screen with AirPlay and even streaming a camera, but nothing beat WebDriverAgent. Stock WebDriverAgent was still slow in a lot of apps, so I patched it and had an agent keep improving it by trying it across tons of apps. That became Turbotap. Now I can just ask AI to change a setting, stress-test my app on a real iPhone, or do something in an app I used to have to do by hand. Honestly, I built it out of irritation and increasing inflammation in my hands, but it’s unlocked so many things I can automate with LLMs. The AI can use the actual iPhone app the same way I would, even if there’s no web version, MCP, or API. That’s why I’m excited to share it. You need Xcode on a Mac to sign and install WebDriverAgent over USB. Once it’s running, you can drive the phone headlessly from a Mac or Linux machine on the same Wi-Fi. It’s free and open source. https://github.com/Maxteabag/turbotap

items.title: Show HN: Plain-Auth an open-source authentication library for Go
items.summary: Hey everyone, I've always loved the simplicity of Go, but the only thing keeping me from switching all of my backends to Go is really one package, and one package only, which is Better-Auth. It's just so easy to use: simple plugin, and start working. It's got everything I need: organizations, teams, billing, social auth, everything. I tried to scour GitHub and the open source community for anything remotely close to it in Go, and I honestly couldn't find anything that was worth it, so I just decided to make it myself. It's an open-source Go package. It is not 100% feature parity with Better-Auth yet, but it's getting there. Would love some feedback. For anyone to try it out, it works with pretty much all of those routers: Chi, Echo, Fiber, Mux and more. Any feedback is greatly appreciated. Oh, and it's also my very first open source repo, so I'm learning as I go.
